Why we moved off Airflow

By Jane Doe, September 20, 2026

For five years our data platform ran on Apache Airflow. It scheduled about 1,200 DAGs every night, and for most of that time it did the job. This post explains why we replaced it with Dagster last spring, what the migration cost, and what we would do differently if we started again tomorrow.

The problem with task-centric orchestration

Airflow thinks in tasks. Our analysts think in tables. Every incident started with the same question: which tables are stale, and which upstream job caused it? Answering that meant reading DAG code, because the scheduler had no idea what data a task produced. Backfills were the worst part: rerunning a month of a single table required clearing dozens of tasks by hand and hoping nothing downstream fired too early.

Results after six months

Moving to asset-based orchestration changed the unit of work from a task to a table. The numbers after six months in production:

MetricBeforeAfter
Failed runs per week4527
Median backfill time3 hours25 minutes

Failures dropped by 40 percent, mostly because freshness checks now run before expensive jobs instead of after them. The migration took two engineers one full quarter.
